t: Maximum Valid Pair Sum — Prefix Maximum Sweep
o: We need the maximum nums[i] + nums[j] over pairs with j - i >= k. A brute force over all pairs is $O(n^2)$, which with n up to 1e5 is too slow (~1e10 operations). The key observation: for each fixed j, we want the maximum nums[i] among indices i <= j - k. So if we sweep j left to right and maintain a running prefix maximum of nums[0..j-k], each pair check is O(1), giving an O(n) solution. In Example 1 (k=2), when j=4 we take the max of nums[0..2]=5, giving 8+5=13; in Example 2 (k=1) every earlier index qualifies, so 9+5=14.
k: For a fixed right index j, only i <= j - k matters, so the best partner is the prefix maximum of nums[0..j-k].
Sweeping j from left to right and maintaining that prefix maximum incrementally yields O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Since k >= 1, valid pairs always exist for j >= k, so no special 'no answer' handling is needed.

a.i: Try every pair (i, j) with j - i >= k and track the maximum sum. This directly mirrors the definition of a valid pair and works fine for small n, but at n = 1e5 it performs up to ~5e9 pair checks, which exceeds time limits.

a.i: Rewrite the objective as max over j of (nums[j] + max(nums[i]) for i <= j - k). As j increases by one, the set of eligible left indices grows by exactly one element, so the eligible maximum can be maintained incrementally. One pass suffices: before processing j, fold nums[j-k] into the running prefix maximum, then combine it with nums[j]. This gives linear time with constant extra space.
s: If j >= k, update prefMax = max(prefMax, nums[j-k]).
If prefMax is set, update ans = max(ans, prefMax + nums[j]).
a.t: O(n) — single pass with O(1) work per element.
a.sp: O(1) — only two scalar variables beyond the input.

w: In an interview, mention brute force briefly to show understanding, then present the prefix-maximum sweep as the intended O(n) solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that sums can reach 2e9 and overflowing 32-bit integers in C++/Java (use long/long long); off-by-one errors on when nums[j-k] becomes eligible (only once j >= k); initializing the answer to 0 is safe here since values are positive, but with negatives you would initialize to negative infinity instead. Edge cases: k = n-1 leaves exactly one pair (0, n-1); k = 1 makes every pair valid. Likely follow-ups: handle negative numbers, return the pair of indices itself (track argmax alongside prefMax), or support online updates (a segment tree over prefix maxima would generalize).
